section.title: The Journey to Jerusalem and Paul's Arrest
section.sectionRationale: Paul sails resolutely toward Jerusalem though the Spirit and the disciples repeatedly warn of chains. In Jerusalem James urges him to join four men in a temple vow to quiet rumors that he teaches Jews to forsake Moses; instead a mob from Asia seizes him on a false charge, and the Roman commander arrests him, opening the long chain of trials that will carry the gospel to Rome.
section.thesis: Set on finishing his course whatever it costs, Paul goes to Jerusalem, takes up James's counsel of a vow to show he honors his people, and is seized on a false accusation, so that his arrest becomes the doorway through which he will testify before governors, kings, and finally in Rome.
section.frameNote: Five movements: the voyage down the coast to Caesarea; Agabus's warning and Paul's resolve; James's counsel and the temple vow; the riot and seizure at the temple; and the Roman rescue with permission to speak.

units.label: The voyage to Caesarea
units.note: warned through the Spirit, farewells on the shore

verses.text: After we had torn ourselves away from them, we sailed directly to Cos, and the next day on to Rhodes, and from there to Patara.
Finding a ship crossing over to Phoenicia, we boarded it and set sail.
After sighting Cyprus and passing south of it, we sailed on to Syria and landed at Tyre, where the ship was to unload its cargo.
We sought out the disciples in Tyre and stayed with them seven days. Through the Spirit they kept telling Paul not to go up to Jerusalem.
But when our time there had ended, we set out on our journey. All the disciples, with their wives and children, accompanied us out of the city and knelt down on the beach to pray with us.
And after we had said our farewells, we went aboard the ship, and they returned home.
When we had finished our voyage from Tyre, we landed at Ptolemais, where we greeted the brothers and stayed with them for a day.
Leaving the next day, we went on to Caesarea and stayed at the home of Philip the evangelist, who was one of the Seven.
He had four unmarried daughters who prophesied.

units.label: Agabus and the resolve to go

verses.text: After we had been there several days, a prophet named Agabus came down from Judea.

Coming over to us, he took Paul’s belt, bound his own feet and hands, and said, “The Holy Spirit says: ‘In this way the Jews of Jerusalem will bind the owner of this belt and hand him over to the Gentiles.’”
When we heard this, we and the people there pleaded with Paul not to go up to Jerusalem.
Then Paul answered, “Why are you weeping and breaking my heart? I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus.”
When he would not be dissuaded, we quieted down and said, “The Lord’s will be done.”
After these days, we packed up and went on to Jerusalem.
Some of the disciples from Caesarea accompanied us, and they took us to stay at the home of Mnason the Cypriot, an early disciple.

units.label: James's counsel and the temple vow

verses.text: When we arrived in Jerusalem, the brothers welcomed us joyfully.
The next day Paul went in with us to see James, and all the elders were present.
Paul greeted them and recounted one by one the things that God had done among the {{ethnos|Gentiles}} through his ministry.
When they heard this, they glorified God. Then they said to Paul, “You see, brother, how many thousands of Jews have believed, and all of them are {{zelotes|zealous}} for the law.
But they are under the impression that you teach all the Jews who live among the Gentiles to forsake Moses, telling them not to circumcise their children or observe our customs.
What then should we do? They will certainly hear that you have come.
Therefore do what we advise you. There are four men with us who have taken a {{euche|vow}}.

Take these men, {{hagnizo|purify}} yourself along with them, and pay their expenses so they can have their heads shaved. Then everyone will know that there is no truth to these rumors about you, but that you also live in obedience to the law.
As for the Gentile believers, we have written to them our decision that they must abstain from food sacrificed to idols, from blood, from the meat of strangled animals, and from sexual immorality.”

So the next day Paul took the men and purified himself along with them. Then he entered the temple to give notice of the date when their purification would be complete and the offering would be made for each of them.

units.label: Seized at the temple
units.note: a false charge, a riot, an arrest

verses.text: When the seven days were almost over, some Jews from the province of Asia saw Paul at the temple. They stirred up the whole crowd and seized him,

crying out, “Men of Israel, help us! This is the man who teaches everyone everywhere against our people and against our law and against this place. Furthermore, he has brought Greeks into the temple and defiled this holy place.”
For they had previously seen Trophimus the Ephesian with him in the city, and they assumed that Paul had brought him into the temple.
The whole city was stirred up, and the people rushed together. They seized Paul and dragged him out of the temple, and at once the gates were shut.
While they were trying to kill him, the commander of the Roman regiment received a report that all Jerusalem was in turmoil.
Immediately he took some soldiers and centurions and ran down to the crowd. When the people saw the commander and the soldiers, they stopped beating Paul.
The commander came up and arrested Paul, ordering that he be bound with two chains. Then he asked who he was and what he had done.
Some in the crowd were shouting one thing, and some another. And since the commander could not get at the truth because of the uproar, he ordered that Paul be brought into the barracks.
When Paul reached the steps, he had to be carried by the soldiers because of the violence of the mob.
For the crowd that followed him kept shouting, “Away with him!”

units.label: Permission to speak
units.note: a citizen of no ordinary city

verses.text: As they were about to take Paul into the barracks, he asked the commander, “May I say something to you?” “Do you speak Greek?” he replied.
“Aren’t you the Egyptian who incited a rebellion some time ago and led four thousand members of the Assassins into the wilderness?”
But Paul answered, “I am a Jew from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no ordinary city. Now I beg you to allow me to speak to the people.”
Having received permission, Paul stood on the steps and motioned to the crowd. A great hush came over the crowd, and he addressed them in Hebrew:

ethnos.gloss: Nation, people; in the plural, the Gentiles, the nations outside Israel. Paul reports what God has done among the ethnē, the very fruit of the mission that Jerusalem struggles to reconcile with zeal for the law.

zelotes.gloss: One who is zealous, a zealot. Thousands of Jewish believers are zealous for the law of Moses; their zeal is real but easily inflamed, and it lies behind the fear that Paul is teaching Jews to abandon their heritage.

euche.gloss: A vow or solemn promise to God, here likely a Nazirite vow with its shaved head and offerings, Numbers 6. James proposes that Paul join and pay for four such men to show publicly that he still honors the law.

hagnizo.gloss: To purify, make ceremonially clean. Paul purifies himself with the four men in the temple, a costly act of goodwill toward Jewish believers; ironically it is in the temple, at the point of this obedience, that he is falsely accused of defiling it.

basic.context: Paul sails down the coast toward Jerusalem, and everywhere the Spirit warns of chains. Friends beg him to turn back; the prophet Agabus acts out his coming arrest with Paul's own belt. Paul will not be moved: he is ready to die for the name of Jesus. In Jerusalem, James welcomes him but reports a rumor that Paul tells Jews to abandon Moses, and urges him to join four men in a temple vow to prove it false. Paul agrees, but a mob from Asia seizes him on a lie, and the Romans arrest him.
basic.hermeneutics: This is narrative that shows more than it commands. Watch two threads: Paul's settled resolve to obey God whatever the cost, and the tangle of law, rumor, and mob that surrounds him. The chapter does not tell us in so many words whether the vow was wise; it lets us weigh it, while making plain that God is steering even the arrest toward His purpose.
basic.originalLanguages: Paul reports what God did among the ethnē, the Gentiles. The Jerusalem believers are zelotai, zealots for the law. James proposes that Paul share a euchē, a vow, and hagnizesthai, purify himself, in the temple. The very act meant to prove his loyalty becomes the setting where enemies accuse him of defiling the holy place.
basic.typology: Paul, bound and handed over to the Gentiles just as Agabus foretold, walks a road that echoes his Lord: Jesus too was warned of, resolved to go up to Jerusalem, and was handed over to the Gentiles. The disciple follows the Master's pattern, though only Christ's binding could atone.
basic.christ: Paul says he is ready to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus. His resolve is not stoic pride but love for Christ and His mission. As Jesus set His face to go to Jerusalem knowing what awaited Him, so Paul goes, and his sufferings will become the means of carrying Christ's name to Rome, just as Christ said they would.
basic.god: God had said Paul would carry His name before Gentiles and kings, and He is now bringing it to pass through a riot and an arrest. The Spirit's warnings are not commands to stop but preparation to stand firm. When friends finally say, The Lord's will be done, they name the truth that governs the whole chapter.
basic.crossReferences: Luke 9:51 shows Jesus setting His face to Jerusalem. Acts 9:15-16 promised Paul would suffer for the name. Numbers 6 gives the Nazirite vow behind the temple rite. Acts 23:11 confirms that God intends this path to reach Rome.
basic.oneStory: The gospel is pressing from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth, and here the road narrows to a prison chain. Paul's arrest looks like defeat, but it is the hinge God uses to send His witness before rulers and, at last, to Rome. The mission advances not around suffering but straight through it.

context.literary:
The chapter is built as a descent. It opens on the sea with a travel log (21:1-8), where the Spirit's warnings are heard in city after city, rises to a single dramatic sign in Caesarea (21:10-14), then runs through two Jerusalem scenes that match each other: a quiet meeting with James and the elders (21:17-26) and a violent scene at the temple (21:27-36). It ends with Paul asking permission to speak and a great hush (21:37-40), which leads straight into the speech of chapter 22. Luke slows the narration at the moments of choice. The farewell on the beach and the sign in Caesarea are told in close detail, and verse 15 then covers the last stretch to Jerusalem in a single line.

One device to notice is the language of binding. In Acts 20:22 Paul says he is going to Jerusalem 'compelled by the Spirit', and the Greek participle literally means bound. In 21:11 Agabus binds his own feet and hands, and says the Jews will bind the owner of the belt. In 21:13 Paul says he is ready to be bound. In 21:33 the Roman commander has him bound with two chains. A single verb thus runs from the Spirit's constraint through the prophecy to the actual shackles, and Luke invites the reader to see that Paul's chains are the Spirit's own path.

The charge against Paul also matches what has gone before. The mob says he teaches against the people, the law and this place (21:28), which repeats the accusation against Stephen in Acts 6:13. The crowd's cry 'Away with him' (21:36) recalls the cry at Jesus's trial in Luke 23:18. The reader is meant to hear that the servant is following his Master and the first martyr, step for step.
context.historical:
The date is around AD 57, shortly before Pentecost. Paul travels with delegates carrying a collection from the Gentile churches, which he had spent years organising, as Romans 15:25-27 and Acts 24:17 show. The voyage hugs the coast: Cos, Rhodes, Patara, then a ship across to Tyre, Ptolemais and Caesarea. Tyre and Caesarea had Christian communities that began with the dispersal after Stephen's death. Philip, who greets them at Caesarea, is one of the seven chosen in Acts 6:5, and his four unmarried daughters who prophesied are a living fulfilment of Joel's promise quoted in Acts 2:17-18. Agabus is the prophet who foretold a famine in Acts 11:28. His acted prophecy with the belt belongs to a long Old Testament tradition of sign acts, such as Isaiah's three years of walking barefoot (Isaiah 20:2-3).

Jerusalem in the fifties was a tense place. Thousands of Jewish believers lived in it, and James says they were all zealous for the law (21:20). Rumour had told them that Paul taught Jews in the Gentile world to abandon Moses, which was untrue; Paul had circumcised Timothy for the sake of the Jews (Acts 16:3), and he had taken a vow himself at Cenchreae (Acts 18:18). James's suggestion is that Paul join four men who had completed a vow of the kind described in Numbers 6, pay for their offerings, and be seen to keep the law. Anyone coming from Gentile lands needed to undergo purification before entering the temple. The 'seven days' in verse 27 fit that process.

The temple court was divided. Gentiles could enter only the outer court, and a stone barrier carried warnings in Greek and Latin that anyone beyond it would be responsible for his own death. A Greek notice of this kind has been recovered by archaeologists. The accusation in verse 28 that Paul had brought Greeks inside was therefore a capital charge in the eyes of the crowd, and Luke tells us it rested on an assumption: they had seen Trophimus the Ephesian in the city and 'assumed' he had been brought in. The Roman garrison was housed in the fortress next to the temple, which is why the commander could reach the scene so quickly. His mistaken guess that Paul was an Egyptian agitator reflects a real recent episode, when a self-styled prophet from Egypt had led crowds into the wilderness.
context.canonical:
This chapter begins the last quarter of Acts, in which the apostle is a prisoner but the word is not bound, as Paul will write from another prison, 2 Timothy 2:9. The sequence of defence speeches before the crowd, the Sanhedrin, Felix, Festus and Agrippa all grow out of the arrest in this chapter. The Lord's promise to Paul at his call in Acts 9:15-16, that he would carry His name before Gentiles and kings and suffer for it, is being fulfilled. So is the Lord's word in Acts 23:11 that Paul must testify in Rome as he has in Jerusalem.

The chapter also serves as a window onto the church's unfinished work of belonging together. Acts 15 had settled that Gentile believers need not be circumcised or keep the whole law, and James repeats the substance of that decision in 21:25. Paul's letters show the matter being worked out from the other side. Galatians 2:3-5 describes how Titus was not compelled to be circumcised, and 1 Corinthians 9:19-23 describes Paul's willingness to become like a Jew to win Jews. Romans 14 and 15 teach the strong to bear with the weak. The vow in Acts 21 is a test case for how those principles are lived.

The pattern of the road to Jerusalem also echoes the Gospel of Luke, by the same author. Jesus 'resolutely set out for Jerusalem' in Luke 9:51, was told that the Son of Man would be delivered over to the Gentiles in Luke 18:32, and was bound and handed over. Luke has written the two journeys in parallel, and the New Testament elsewhere says that believers who follow Him must take up a cross. Paul himself, in the letter he wrote just before this journey, asked the Roman believers to pray that he would be delivered from unbelievers in Judea and that his service in Jerusalem would be acceptable, Romans 15:30-31, and Luke shows how that prayer was heard.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Luke is answering a charge that a reader in the Roman world might well have heard: that Paul was a troublemaker, a lawbreaker and an enemy of the Jewish people. He shows the opposite. Paul arrives in Jerusalem carrying a gift for the poor, reports what God has done among the Gentiles, is welcomed with joy, and agrees to a plan designed to show that he lives in obedience to the law. The riot comes from a rumour and a mistaken assumption, not from anything he did. The Roman commander himself, when he questions him, finds an educated man from a great city.

Luke also intends the reader to see that Paul goes up to Jerusalem knowing the cost. The warnings are plain, the friends weep, and Paul does not turn back, yet he is not reckless. He is bound by the Spirit, as Luke's wording suggests, and he gives his reason: the name of the Lord Jesus. The closing words of his friends, 'The Lord's will be done', are meant to be heard as the settling of the matter. The narrative's quiet claim is that God's will can include suffering, and that obedience is not measured by whether things go well.

There is a pastoral purpose as well. Many believers who read Acts would be wondering whether suffering means they have taken a wrong turn. Luke shows that a faithful servant can be imprisoned, misunderstood and mobbed, and that none of this means God has stopped governing. Paul's arrest is not the end of his ministry but the next stage of it.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription: Almost everything in the chapter is description: the route, the hospitality, the prophecy of Agabus, the vow, the riot. Luke does not command believers to take Nazirite-type vows, to expect prophetic sign acts, or to travel into danger because a prophet predicts it. The chapter also does not say that the Spirit's warning at Tyre was a command to Paul to stay away, or that Paul was right to go; it records both the warning and Paul's refusal and lets the later narrative show how God used the outcome.\n\nWhat carries forward is the quality of Paul's response. He is ready to be bound and to die for the name of the Lord Jesus, and he refuses to let affection, even a loving friend's tears, decide what he owes his Lord. He is also ready to bend on matters that do not touch the gospel, in order not to cause needless offence, which is the teaching of 1 Corinthians 9:19-23 lived out. The friends' last word, 'The Lord's will be done', is a prayer that every believer can imitate when a decision cannot be changed. The practice of Christians who accompany a missionary to the shore, kneel and pray on the beach, and then let him go (21:5-6) is another thing to take away without making it a rule.

debates.question: Was Paul right to take the temple vow at James's urging?

views.label: Yes, a wise and loving accommodation
views.case: Paul had written that to the Jews he became as a Jew to win them, 1 Corinthians 9:20, and the vow denied no gospel truth; it simply showed he did not despise his heritage. The strongest case is that Paul acted in love to protect the unity of Jewish and Gentile believers, and Luke records no divine rebuke.

views.label: No, an unwise compromise
views.case: Some judge that Paul, the apostle of freedom from the law, bent too far to pressure and blurred the very liberty Galatians defends, and that the plan failed and landed him in chains. The strongest case is that the scheme did not achieve its aim and that appeasing the zealots risked confusing the gospel. They add that the rite of Numbers 6:13-20 includes a sin offering, which sits uneasily with a faith that rests on Christ's one sacrifice, Hebrews 10:1-4.

debates.bearing: How we read the vow shapes how we handle Christian liberty: whether we may freely accommodate scruples for the sake of peace and mission, as long as no gospel truth is surrendered, or whether such accommodation endangers the freedom Christ won.

debates.question: Did Paul disobey the Spirit by going to Jerusalem?

views.label: No, the Spirit warned of what was coming and Paul was right to go on
views.case: Acts 20:22-23 says Paul was compelled by the Spirit and that the Holy Spirit warned him of chains in town after town. The disciples at Tyre said 'through the Spirit' not to go up, but Luke does not say that the Spirit forbade it. The Lord later stood by Paul in prison and told him to take courage, Acts 23:11, which is hard to imagine if Paul had defied Him. The strongest case is that the disciples drew a loving but wrong conclusion from a true warning.

views.label: Yes, Paul went against the Spirit's guidance at Tyre
views.case: Luke's own words say that the Tyre disciples spoke through the Spirit, and Paul went anyway. Some read this as a sign that Paul's zeal outran his guidance, and that his imprisonment followed from it. The strongest case is the plain wording of 21:4 and the fact that Paul's plan to appease the Jerusalem believers did not work.

debates.bearing: The answer shapes how we think about guidance. If the first view is right, the Spirit sometimes shows us a cost without telling us to avoid it, and faithfulness can mean walking into what He has warned of. The Lord's later words to Paul and the way the story serves the gospel make this the more natural reading.

study.originalLanguages:
A few Greek details shed light on the chapter. The disciples at Tyre said 'through the Spirit' that Paul should not go up to Jerusalem (21:4). Luke uses the preposition dia, through. The question is whether the Spirit supplied the warning of danger or the instruction to stay away, and the grammar alone does not decide it. It means the Spirit was the channel of the message. What the disciples made of it is another matter.

By contrast, Paul's statement in 20:22 uses a participle, dedemenos, which means bound. He is bound in the Spirit, and then Agabus uses the same family of words for the binding of the belt's owner, desousin, in 21:11. When Paul says he is ready 'not only to be bound' in 21:13, the infinitive is dethenai. Luke has strung a single verb through the whole travelogue and made it the thread by which the reader sees that the Spirit's binding and the Jews' binding meet in the same road. Agabus's gesture of tying his own feet and hands with Paul's belt, perhaps the long sash worn at the waist, is what the prophets of the Old Testament would have called an acted oracle.

In 21:14 the friends say 'The Lord's will be done'. The Greek is tou kyriou to thelema ginestho, with the imperative ginestho, let it be done, and this is the same imperative Jesus used in Gethsemane, Luke 22:42, 'Yet not My will, but Yours be done'. Luke does not draw attention to the echo, and the reader is meant to catch it. Paul's friends are speaking the prayer Jesus prayed on the night before the cross.

In verse 20 the BSB says 'how many thousands' have believed. The Greek word is muriades, which literally means tens of thousands, and it was used loosely for a very large number. The word zelotai, zealots for the law, describes people eager and jealous to protect the law, and Paul himself used the same word for his former life, Galatians 1:14. The rumour in verse 21 uses the noun apostasia, the source of our word apostasy, when it says that Paul teaches Jews to abandon Moses. It is a heavy word, and it explains why James thinks a public sign is needed. The same verse uses katecheo for 'they are under the impression', literally they have been told or instructed, the root of the word catechism. They were fed a line about Paul and they believed it.

Finally, in 21:39 Paul calls Tarsus a city of no ordinary kind, using the adjective asemos, which meant undistinguished or unmarked, and with the negative it is a polite boast. His question to the commander, 'Do you know Greek?', translates a single word, Hellenisti, which is the adverb 'in Greek'. The question tells us how the soldier had read Paul. The surprise is that Paul could speak well, and that when he turns to the crowd he switches to the local language.

typology.fulfillment: The prophets often acted their message before they spoke it. Isaiah walked barefoot for three years as a sign against Egypt, Isaiah 20:2-3, and Jeremiah hid and dug up a linen loincloth to show what God would do to the pride of Judah, Jeremiah 13:1-11. Agabus takes Paul's belt and binds himself, so that the audience sees what the words will say. The correspondence is the use of an object as a sermon. The escalation is that Agabus's sign is not a warning to repent but a revelation of what the Spirit has already appointed for the apostle, and it is fulfilled to the letter. The type falls short because the prophets' signs pointed at a nation's judgment, while this one points at a messenger's suffering for the gospel.

typology.type: Bound and delivered to the Gentiles, Acts 21:11 and 21:33
typology.fulfillment: Jesus told the Twelve that the Son of Man would be delivered over to the Gentiles, mocked, flogged and killed, Luke 18:32-33. Paul is bound by Jews and handed over to the Gentiles, in the very words Agabus uses. The correspondence is a pattern of passion: Jerusalem, a Jewish accusation, Roman hands, and chains. The escalation is that Paul's bonds, unlike those of his Lord, are not redemptive. Christ was bound and bore sin, and Paul is bound and bears witness and his sufferings serve the church without paying for it. The type falls short precisely where Christ's work is unrepeatable: Paul can follow, but he cannot atone.

typology.type: The vow and the offerings of Numbers 6
typology.fulfillment: The Nazirite law ended in the temple with burnt, sin and peace offerings and the shaving of the head, Numbers 6:13-20. James asks Paul to pay for four men to complete such a vow and to join them. The sacrificial system was a shadow of the good things to come, Hebrews 10:1, and could not take away sins, Hebrews 10:4. The escalation is that Christ's single offering fulfils what those offerings pointed toward. The type falls short in the way Hebrews sees it: any sacrifice that could be repeated could not be the final one. Luke does not explain how Paul thought of the offerings, and we should avoid reading more into the scene than he gives.

typology.type: The Lord's will be done, Acts 21:14
typology.fulfillment: Jesus's prayer in Gethsemane, 'Yet not My will, but Yours be done', Luke 22:42, becomes the prayer of Paul's friends on the road to Jerusalem. The correspondence is the same surrender in the face of a cost that cannot be avoided. The escalation is that Jesus prayed it at the threshold of the cross itself, where the whole of salvation depended on the answer, while Paul's friends pray it on behalf of a servant whose suffering follows a path that has already been cut. The type falls short because the friends submit to a will they only partly understand, while Christ submitted fully knowing what the cup contained.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ most plainly through Paul's reason for going. He is ready not only to be bound but to die in Jerusalem 'for the name of the Lord Jesus'. This is not stoicism or the pride of a man who cannot back down. It is the language of someone who has been told what the name is worth. The Lord said at Paul's call that he would carry His name before Gentiles and kings and that he would suffer for it, Acts 9:15-16, and Paul now sees those two promises moving together. To carry the name is to carry the cost.

The chapter is also written to be read beside the story of Jesus Himself. Luke 9:51 says Jesus resolutely set out for Jerusalem, and Luke 18:31-33 spells out what would happen there. In Acts 21 the same sequence returns: a determined journey, warnings from those who love him, a handing over to the Gentiles, a Jewish crowd crying 'Away with him', and a Roman commander. Luke does not say that Paul is a second Christ. He says that the servant's road is shaped by the Master's, and that the pattern of the Master is what gives the servant courage. The one who was bound and led away has gone before.

The law enters the picture too. The believers in Jerusalem are zealous for it, and James asks Paul to demonstrate that he too walks in it. Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes, Romans 10:4, which means that the law's whole purpose is gathered up in Him, and that Jewish believers who keep it do so as a heritage and not as a way of being saved. The vow and its offerings point forward to Christ's sacrifice, as Hebrews 10 explains. Paul's willingness to take part, without surrendering the gospel, is a picture of how a person can honour what the law pointed toward while knowing the One to whom it pointed.

There is also a quiet echo of Christ's patience with the weak. Paul writes in Romans 15:1-3 that the strong should bear with the weak, because even Christ did not please Himself. The vow in Jerusalem is one place where he does it. It would be wrong to claim that every detail of the chapter is a figure of Christ. What the text supports is that the servant's whole bearing here, his resolve, his gentleness to the zealous, and his readiness to be handed over, derives from his Lord, and that the Lord is Himself the reason for all of it.
study.god:
God is the quiet main actor of this chapter. He is not named in most of the scenes, which are filled with ships, crowds and soldiers, but every turn runs through His purposes. The Spirit speaks through the disciples at Tyre and through Agabus. The Lord had told Paul at his call that he would suffer for His name, and He will tell him in prison that he must testify in Rome. The path that the chapter traces from the harbour to the barracks is the path God said He would take.

The chapter holds together two truths that often seem to pull against each other. God warns of suffering, and God sends His servant into it. A Spirit who reveals danger might be expected to reveal a way around it. Instead He tells the cost and leaves the servant free to choose obedience, and then He stays with him. This is a different kind of guidance from the one that gives a map of safe roads. It is guidance that gives a companion for a hard one. The friends who weep are not rebuked, and the apostle who will not be dissuaded is not praised for stubbornness. Luke lets both stand.

The chapter also shows God's sovereignty over unjust institutions without excusing the injustice. The mob is wrong, the rumour is false, the accusation is a lie, and yet the rescue comes from a Roman officer who knew nothing about Paul and acted out of a concern for order. God uses the soldiers who run down the steps, and the crowd's own violence puts Paul in the position to address Jerusalem. He does not need people's goodwill to do His work. He can use the hand that is raised against His servant to carry him to the place of testimony.

For worship, the passage invites the believer to learn the prayer of verse 14. It is not resignation. It is the confidence of people who know that the will of the Lord is good, that it has been tested in the life of His Son, and that it can be asked for even when it will cost a friend dearly. The disciples kneeling on the beach at Tyre with their children (21:5) are as much a picture of worship as any temple service, and the temple court in this chapter, where worship is shattered by a riot, is a reminder that the true shelter of God's people is not a building but the God who keeps them.

crossReferences.note: Jesus resolutely sets out for Jerusalem knowing what waits there. Luke, the author of Acts, tells Paul's journey in the same shape, with warnings, a determined servant, a mob and a handing over. The parallel is the strongest evidence that Acts 21 is meant to be read beside the Gospel.

At Paul's call the Lord says he will carry His name before Gentiles and kings and that he will be shown how much he must suffer for it. Acts 21 is where the two halves of that promise meet. The warnings of the Spirit are the Lord's own word coming true, not a sign that something has gone wrong.

Paul says he became like a Jew to win the Jews and like one under the law to win those under the law, though he himself is not. This is the best explanation of why he accepts James's proposal in Acts 21:23-26. He treats the vow as a means to the gospel's progress and not as a requirement of righteousness.

The Lord stands by Paul in the barracks and tells him to take courage, for as he has testified in Jerusalem he must testify in Rome. It confirms that the journey and the arrest are within God's plan and answers the question whether Paul should have gone. The heavenly word follows the earthly chains.

Jesus prays in Gethsemane that the Father's will be done, using the same imperative that Paul's friends use in Acts 21:14. The words come from the lips of those who cannot stop their friend and choose to leave him in God's hands. They are borrowing the prayer of the Lord on the eve of the cross.

Jesus tells the Twelve that He will be delivered over to the Gentiles and mocked, flogged and killed. Agabus's prophecy that Paul will be bound by the Jews and handed over to the Gentiles in Acts 21:11 uses the same words. The disciple is walking the road his Lord walked first.

The Nazirite law lays out the completion of a vow: offerings at the Tent of Meeting, the shaving of the consecrated head and the burning of the hair. This is the background to James's suggestion that Paul pay for the four men so they can have their heads shaved. It also reminds us that the rite included a sin offering.

The Jerusalem council's letter to the Gentile believers asks only that they abstain from food sacrificed to idols, from blood, from strangled meat and from sexual immorality. James repeats it to Paul in 21:25, which shows that the plan about the vow does not reopen the question of Gentile obligation. The decision stands.

The false witnesses against Stephen said he never stopped speaking against this holy place and against the law. The crowd's charge against Paul in 21:28 repeats it. Luke makes the connection so that readers see Paul entering the same fire that Stephen entered, with Saul now on the other side.

Written shortly before this journey, Paul begs the Romans to pray that he will be delivered from the unbelievers in Judea and that his service in Jerusalem will be acceptable to the saints. Acts 21 shows both prayers being answered in unexpected ways, with deliverance coming through a Roman officer and acceptance coming through a welcome from James.

Isaiah went barefoot and stripped of his outer garments for three years as a sign against Egypt and Cush. It is one of the best known sign acts of the Old Testament and the background for Agabus's use of Paul's belt. The prophetic tradition did not only speak; it acted what it said.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story is repeatedly about a servant who goes where he is sent although it will cost him, so that others may be blessed. Abraham leaves his country. Joseph goes to Egypt as a slave and is raised up to save many. Moses returns to Pharaoh. Isaiah's Servant is despised and rejected and yet will bring light to the nations. The pattern comes to its centre in Jesus, who sets His face toward Jerusalem. Acts 21 is a small scene in that long line. Paul is not the Servant, but he serves the Servant, and the chains he is about to wear belong to the same story.

The chapter also turns on a question that has run through Acts from chapter 10: how can Jews and Gentiles be one people? Peter's vision, Cornelius's household, the council in Acts 15 and Paul's collection all aim at the same thing, a single body drawn from both. In Acts 21 the aim is tested at the temple. Paul brings gifts from the Gentiles, James welcomes the news, and then the barrier meant to divide the courts of the temple becomes the pretext for violence. The scene is a small picture of the problem Ephesians 2:14 later says Christ solved when He broke down the dividing wall. Paul will later say that in Christ the dividing wall of hostility has been broken down.

The arrest also leads forward. Paul will stand before the crowd, the Council, two governors and a king. He will appeal to Caesar and sail for Rome. The mission Jesus announced in Acts 1:8, to the ends of the earth, will reach Rome through the chain that this chapter fastens on Paul. What looks like the end of his travelling is the means by which he reaches the capital.

The end of the story is the city where there is no temple and no barrier. Revelation 21 describes a Jerusalem whose gates are never shut, with the nations walking by its light. Paul's gates in Acts 21:30 are shut against him, a sign of a world still divided, and the barrier warning stood at the edge of the very court where this happened. The new creation reverses the scene: the gates stand open, the nations enter, and nothing unclean is kept in or out by a riot, because the Lamb is the temple of that city.

quiz.q: Why did Paul keep going to Jerusalem despite the warnings?

options.text: He was ready to be bound and to die for the name of the Lord Jesus.
options.note: Paul says exactly this in verse 13, showing his resolve to obey whatever the cost.

options.text: He wanted to report to James and the elders what God had done.
options.note: He did report to James, but his stated reason for pressing on was his readiness to suffer for Christ's name.

options.text: He hoped the warnings would prove exaggerated.
options.note: The reverse: he took the warnings seriously and went anyway, ready for chains and death.

options.text: He was under Roman orders to appear in the city.
options.note: No such order existed; his arrest by Rome comes only after he arrives.

quiz.q: Why did James urge Paul to join the four men in a temple vow?

options.text: To show publicly that Paul still honored the law and had not told Jews to forsake Moses.
options.note: James names this aim: to disprove the rumor and show Paul lives in obedience to the law.

options.text: To keep peace among the thousands of Jewish believers zealous for the law.
options.note: True and part of the motive, but the specific purpose was to refute the rumor about Paul by a public sign.

options.text: To require Gentile believers to keep the whole law of Moses.
options.note: The opposite: James reaffirms the earlier decision that Gentiles keep only a few essentials.

options.text: To punish Paul for preaching to the Gentiles.
options.note: James and the elders glorified God for Paul's Gentile ministry; the vow was not a punishment.

quiz.q: What was the accusation that sparked the riot?

options.text: That Paul taught against the people and the law and had brought a Greek into the temple.
options.note: The Asian Jews charged him on both counts, the temple charge based on a false assumption about Trophimus.

options.text: That Paul had brought a Gentile past the barrier into the temple.
options.note: This was the inflaming charge, but the accusers also charged him with teaching against people, law, and place.

options.text: That Paul had stolen from the temple treasury.
options.note: No theft is charged; the accusation concerned teaching and defiling the temple.

options.text: That Paul had denied that Jesus is the Messiah.
options.note: The charge was the opposite sort; nothing here concerns denying Christ.

quiz.q: How does the chapter show God's hand in Paul's arrest?

options.text: The arrest fulfills the warnings and becomes the road by which Paul will witness to rulers and reach Rome.
options.note: The Spirit foretold the chains, and Acts shows them as God's chosen path to Rome.

options.text: The Roman commander rescued Paul from the mob just in time.
options.note: True and providential, but it understates the larger design: the arrest itself serves God's mission.

options.text: God kept Paul from any suffering at all.
options.note: Paul was beaten and bound; God's purpose ran through the suffering, not around it.

options.text: The arrest ended Paul's usefulness for the gospel.
options.note: The opposite: it opened his greatest platform, before governors, a king, and finally Rome.

quiz.q: How did the friends respond when Paul would not be dissuaded?

options.text: They stopped urging him and said, The Lord's will be done.
options.note: They surrendered to God's will, echoing Christ's own prayer in Gethsemane.

options.text: They wept and pleaded with him not to go up to Jerusalem.
options.note: They did weep and plead at first, but their final word was submission to the Lord's will.

options.text: They abandoned Paul and refused to travel with him.
options.note: The reverse: some disciples accompanied him on to Jerusalem.

options.text: They forced Paul to change his plans.
options.note: Paul could not be dissuaded, and they yielded to him and to God's will.

questions: Paul was ready not only to be bound but to die for the name of Jesus. What would it look like for you to hold your own life loosely for the sake of Christ?
The disciples' warnings came through the Spirit, yet Paul still went. How do you discern between a warning about hardship and a command to turn back?
James asked Paul to accommodate the scruples of Jewish believers without surrendering the gospel. Where might love call you to yield your freedom for the sake of others?
The very act meant to prove Paul's goodwill led to his arrest. How do you keep trusting God when doing the right thing seems to make matters worse?
When they could not change Paul's mind, the friends prayed, The Lord's will be done. Where do you need to come to that same rest today?
Paul's chains became the road to Rome. Where might God be working through a hardship in your life in a way you cannot yet see?

translationNotes.note: Addressed them in Hebrew carries a footnoted alternative, in Aramaic; literally in the Hebrew language. It names the local language of the Jerusalem crowd.
The vow with its shaved heads and offerings is best understood as a Nazirite vow, Numbers 6; Paul pays the expenses of the four men to help them complete it.
The Assassins renders the term for the sicarii, dagger-carrying rebels of the period; the commander first mistakes Paul for a known Egyptian insurgent.
